candidates.attacker_control: Arguments to the public JDBC API DatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges(catalog, schemaPattern, tableNamePattern). These are client-supplied pattern strings; database tools, schema-diff/permission viewers and applications commonly derive them from user input (table name search / catalog browsing), so an application that forwards untrusted text here hands the attacker the SQL text that is concatenated verbatim.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that other metadata methods in the same file do escape patterns (escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand for LIKE, escapeSqlQuotes for double-quoted identifiers), so this is an inconsistent omission rather than a global design choice; verified unescapeChars/escapeSqlQuotes implementations show single quotes are never escaped; verified the sink really executes the concatenated string (statement.executeQuery); verified the method is public/reachable and not gated by a session flag; considered that the caller (not the driver) usually owns the input, which limits exploitability; considered that multi-statement execution is not supported by the driver/API, capping impact.
candidates.impact: SQL injection inside a SELECT executed with the connection's privileges. An injected quote lets the caller alter the WHERE clause (e.g., bypass the intended table/schema scoping and read other rows of table_privileges) or append set operations/subqueries to read other tables the session can access, i.e., metadata/data disclosure beyond the intended lookup. Because Snowflake's query API does not accept multiple statements in one call, the practical impact is single-statement read manipulation rather than arbitrary DDL/DML or privilege escalation.
candidates.prerequisites: An established Snowflake connection (any authenticated role), and an application/tool that passes attacker-influenced text as tableNamePattern (or schemaPattern) to getTablePrivileges. tableNamePattern must be non-null/non-'%' to reach the concatenation (line 1985-1990).
candidates.root_cause: getTablePrivileges builds a SELECT against information_schema.table_privileges by direct string concatenation. tableNamePattern is interpolated raw inside a single-quoted literal (line 1989: " where table_name = '" + tableNamePattern + "'"), and schemaPattern is passed through unescapeChars (lines 1997/1999), but unescapeChars only unescapes LIKE wildcards and then calls escapeSqlQuotes, which doubles double quotes (lines 238-250) — it does not escape single quotes. Both values therefore terminate the '...' string literal. The resulting SQL is executed unchanged by executeAndReturnEmptyResultIfNotFound -> statement.executeQuery(sql) (lines 3657-3665). This is inconsistent with sibling methods in the same file that escape user-supplied patterns (escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand, escapeSqlQuotes in identifier contexts).
candidates.title: SQL injection via unescaped table/schema patterns in SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges
candidates.trace: caller -> SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges (line 1956, @Override public) -> string building at line 1989 (raw tableNamePattern in single quotes) and lines 1997/1999 (schemaPattern after unescapeChars, which only escapes double quotes) -> executeAndReturnEmptyResultIfNotFound (line 2008-2009) -> statement.executeQuery(showView) at line 3665 -> Snowflake executes the altered SELECT with the session's privileges.
candidates.unverified: No build/run or dynamic test was performed, so exploitability of a concrete payload and the exact Snowflake grammar behavior were not runtime-confirmed. Whether callers in practice pass untrusted input to this JDBC method is application-dependent. Whether this file region differs from the released upstream 3.21.1 source could not be checked (no network/git history available).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-89 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

coverage_summary: Scope: 345 visible source files (283 Java under src/main, plus build/CI/pom files); no test sources were present. get_source_scope reports no exclusions/symlink trimming and a 5 MiB per-file text limit (none hit). The P1 relation index is partial: 319 files indexed, only 37 parsed for symbols/calls, 26 source files absent from the index, 18,373 call rows/17,289 edges, and it explicitly does not implement control/data-flow, semantic resolution, runtime reachability, or exploitability; I used it only for navigation and verified every cited location in source text. I read in depth the metadata layer (SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData, DBMetadataResultSetMetadata, ResultSet wrappers), auth/login (SessionUtil, SessionUtilExternalBrowser, SessionUtilKeyPair, SFSession*, auth package), TLS/OCSP (SFTrustManager, SFSSLConnectionSocketFactory, diagnostic checks), HTTP/retry (HttpUtil, RestRequest, StmtUtil), credential/cache/storage (SecureStorage*Manager, FileCacheManager, SecretDetector), file transfer and cloud storage clients (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent, S3/GCS/Azure clients, EncryptionProvider/GcmEncryptionProvider), result/chunk parsing (SnowflakeChunkDownloader, ResultJsonParserV2, Arrow converters), and the loader package. Remaining Java files (notably parts of SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData 3.6k lines, SnowflakeFileTransferAgent 3.4k lines, SFStatement/SFSession and some Arrow/decimal converters) were only sampled/searched, not exhaustively line-reviewed.
limitations: No compilation, test execution, scanner run, or dynamic confirmation was performed; findings are static source reasoning only.

The relation index is partial (37/283 Java files parsed for symbols, 26 files missing) and provides no data-flow or reachability proof; index 'security_call' and other facts are name-based hints only.

No git history, release artifacts, or external advisories/CVE data were available (and not permitted), so I could not confirm whether the cited code matches the released upstream 3.21.1 source or which fix commit the snapshot precedes.

Exploitability of the candidate depends on application behavior (passing untrusted strings to DatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges) and on Snowflake SQL grammar for injected single statements; neither was runtime-verified.
Dependency-level issues (parent-pom dependency versions) and generated/vendored artifacts were not assessed as vulnerabilities.
Build/CI scripts, FIPS packaging files, and the javadoc licenses page were not security-reviewed in depth.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand (lines 258-274): the helper skips quotes immediately preceded by a backslash, so a pattern containing an even number of backslashes before a quote (e.g. "x\\'") can terminate the LIKE literal used by getTables/getColumns/getSchemas/getProcedures/getStreams.
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking edge case, but exploitation needs a specific backslash sequence and the injected text must still fit the SHOW ... LIKE grammar; the raw interpolation in getTablePrivileges is a clearer, unconditional omission, so I kept one candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeConnectionV1.setCatalog (line 441) and setSchema (lines 758-760) concatenate catalog/schema names into "use database" / "use schema" quoted identifiers without escaping embedded double quotes.
rejected_leads.reason: Identifiers are double-quoted and inputs normally come from pool/config rather than untrusted data; impact limited to the USE grammar. Possible injection anti-pattern, not selected as the strongest evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeConnectionV1.downloadStream (lines 1016-1049) wraps a stage path in single quotes for special characters but never escapes embedded single quotes, and embeds Pattern.quote(fileName) inside a double-quoted PATTERN option where '"' is not neutralized, before the GET command is parsed/executed via SFStatement.executeHelper.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible command/SQL injection through a public API, but it depends on the caller passing attacker-influenced file names (e.g. git-stage content) and on GS GET-command grammar; less directly evidenced than cand-1.

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeBasicDataSource.readObject/readObjectHelper (lines 60-86) deserialize seven fields with ObjectInputStream and no ObjectInputFilter; the class is Serializable and holds credentials.
rejected_leads.reason: Unsafe only if an application deserializes attacker-supplied bytes into this class; the driver itself never deserializes untrusted data, so no in-library exploit path is visible.
ssoUrl is validated by URLUtil.isValidURL against a restrictive regex (no shell metacharacters/whitespace) and Runtime.exec(String) does not invoke a shell, so command injection is not demonstrated.

rejected_leads.lead: FileTransferAgent download path builds local files as localLocation + separator + server-provided basename (manifest FileMetadata.destFileName, SnowflakeS3Client/SnowflakeGCSClient download), with no canonical-path check.
rejected_leads.reason: destFileName is reduced to the substring after the last '/' so ordinary traversal is stripped; a Windows-only backslash traversal via malicious server data is conceivable but is not verifiable here and was kept out of the top candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SecureStorageLinuxManager/FileCacheManager store OAuth/ID tokens in a plaintext JSON file without explicit 0600 permissions; SFClientConfigParser only warns (TODO SNOW-1503722) when a config/token file is group/other-writable.
rejected_leads.reason: Design-level hardening gaps noted in the code itself (warnings/TODOs), not a demonstrated exploitable vulnerability in this snapshot.

summary: Reviewed the assigned snowflake-jdbc 3.21.1-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (345 visible files, 283 Java files under src/main plus build/CI files) as a defensive source review. I traced attacker-controlled input through authentication (SessionUtil/SessionUtilExternalBrowser/SessionUtilKeyPair), TLS/OCSP validation (SFTrustManager, SFSSLConnectionSocketFactory), HTTP plumbing (HttpUtil, RestRequest), credential/caching (SecureStorage*, FileCacheManager, SecretDetector), file transfer (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent and cloud storage clients), result/chunk handling, and the JDBC metadata layer. The strongest, most concrete source-level issue is in SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges: unlike its sibling metadata methods, it concatenates the caller-supplied table and schema patterns into a single-quoted SQL literal without neutralizing single quotes, then executes the string via statement.executeQuery. Other suspicious spots (Runtime.exec of the SSO URL, Java serialization in SnowflakeBasicDataSource, unescaped identifiers in setCatalog/setSchema and downloadStream, the backslash edge case in escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand) were examined and are weaker or plausibly mitigated; they are listed only as rejected leads. No code was executed and no runtime verification was performed; all conclusions are from source text plus index navigation hints.
